Analysis: Both hypotheses are novel in integrating gut microbiota, bile acid metabolism, and cancer stem cell biology, but they differ in their target tissues and translational angles. Hypothesis 1, linking a high‐fat diet with increased hydrophobic bile acids that trigger TGR5/FXR‐mediated epigenetic reprogramming in colonic cells, offers a comprehensive mechanistic framework for colorectal cancer initiation. Despite some gaps in detailing the epigenetic cascade and in clearly defining cancer stem cell markers, its components are rooted in established links between diet, microbiota dysbiosis, and colon cancer. In contrast, Hypothesis 2 leverages gut microbiota modulation to elevate hydrophilic bile acids (UDCA) to reprogram receptor signaling in breast cancer cells in a tumor-suppressive manner. While its therapeutic premise is attractive and may have a favorable safety profile given UDCA’s known properties, it faces challenges regarding the quantitative bioavailability of UDCA in breast tissue and the clarity of its mechanistic pathway. In terms of testability, Hypothesis 1 appears more directly aligned with current experimental models using dietary interventions and multi-omics analyses, whereas Hypothesis 2 demands rigorous pharmacodynamic studies to verify systemic and tissue-specific effects. Overall, Hypothesis 1 is more plausible and readily testable despite needing further mechanistic refinement.
